prompt: Which of these is one of the three rules of the Kubernetes network model?
hint: The opposite of what Docker does by default.

choices.text: Pods reach each other through their node's address and a published port
choices.why: That is Docker's default; Kubernetes asks for no translation between pods.

choices.text: Every pod reaches every other pod at its own address
choices.why: Right: on any node, with no address translation in between.

choices.text: Pods on different nodes must use a Service to talk
choices.why: `left` pinged `right` directly by its pod address.

choices.text: Every pod shares its node's IP address
choices.why: Each pod had its own address from its node's slice.

prompt: The reply to `left`'s ping came back with `ttl=62`. What does that say about the path?

choices.text: The packet was wrapped in a tunnel
choices.why: A tunnel would hide its hops; the TTL counts routers that decremented it.
`0% packet loss`.

choices.text: It was routed twice, once by each node
choices.why: Right: 64 minus two routing hops.
TTL counts down from its starting value, here 64.

prompt: On `shop-worker`, a new pod gets an address. Which one could it be?
hint: Each node hands out addresses from its own slice.

choices.why: That is `shop-worker2`'s slice.
Right: `shop-worker`'s POD-CIDR is `10.244.2.0/24`.
That is the nodes' own network, not a pod range.
That range is for Services.

prompt: What did kindnet write on `shop-worker` so that `left` could reach `right`?

choices.text: A VXLAN tunnel to every other node
choices.why: There is no tunnel interface in the routes.
Pod-to-pod traffic here needs only routes.
Names are not involved; the ping used an address.
Right: one route per other node's slice.

choices.why: Those need every node on one network that carries pod addresses.

choices.text: More Services in front of the pods
choices.why: Services still need pod-to-pod reachability underneath.
Without one, pods get no network at all.
